samples.summary: PKCE downgrade: a code minted without a challenge redeems even when the client presents a `codeVerifier` (RFC 7636 §4.6 violation), so the "two independent bindings" collapse to the nonce alone
samples.evidence: `consumeCode` only checks the verifier when `entry.codeChallenge` is set (cli-auth.store.ts:115). It never checks the converse — a code whose state carried NO `code_challenge` is redeemed for anyone who holds it, even though the caller supplied a verifier. RFC 7636 §4.6 requires the token endpoint to fail in exactly that case. Attack: (1) attacker learns the victim's loopback port and nonce (both are printed verbatim by the CLI at login.ts:57 `Opening browser: ${oauthUrl}` — stderr that this product's own docs tell agents/CI to capture — and both land in backend access logs via the pino `req.url` serializer, app.module.ts:68); (2) attacker opens `GET /auth/github?mode=cli&port=<victim-port>&nonce=<victim-nonce>` with **no** `code_challenge` and completes GitHub consent as themselves; (3) the backend mints an unchallenged code and redirects to `http://127.0.0.1:<victim-port>/callback?code=X&state=<victim-nonce>` (auth.controller.ts:130-135), and any page in the victim's browser can be made to issue that loopback GET; (4) the victim's CLI accepts it (state matches, login.ts:241) and POSTs `{code:X, codeVerifier:<victim verifier>}`; (5) the exchange ignores the verifier because the entry has no challenge and returns the ATTACKER's tokens (auth.controller.ts:166-177), so the victim's terminal — and every subsequent `wafflebase` write — is silently bound to the attacker's account. The docs assert PKCE is an independent defence here (docs/design/rest-api.md:382, cli.md "PKCE ... independently makes an intercepted code unredeemable"), which this gap makes false. Fix: reject when `codeVerifier` is present but the entry has no challenge (and consider requiring a challenge outright for `mode=cli`).

samples.summary: A malformed/over-long `code_challenge` is silently dropped and the CLI login proceeds with no PKCE binding at all, undetectably to the client
samples.evidence: `boundedToken` returns `undefined` for a challenge outside 43–128 chars or the base64url alphabet (github-auth.guard.ts:25-28), and the guard then calls `createState(mode, portNum, nonce, undefined)` (line 56-66) — i.e. the flow continues as an unchallenged, bearer-only code instead of failing the authorization request. Nothing on the wire tells the CLI that its challenge was discarded, and the exchange accepts the code without a verifier (cli-auth.store.ts:115). This is reachable in the documented headless path (`docs/design/cli.md`: "also prints URL for copy-paste"), where a URL truncated at the terminal edge loses the trailing `code_challenge=` but keeps `nonce=`, silently downgrading a login that the user believes is PKCE-protected. Combined with the missing verifier-without-challenge rejection above, the downgrade is unobservable at both ends. A rejected/absent challenge on a `mode=cli` request should be a 400, not a silent drop.

samples.summary: The rewritten "OAuth state forgery (CSRF)" risk row claims a state token is minted "per OAuth request", but the guard mints one only for `mode=cli`; the browser login still sends no `state` to GitHub, so web login CSRF stays unmitigated
samples.evidence: `GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate` only calls `createState` inside `if (mode === 'cli' && port)` (github-auth.guard.ts:53). `GitHubStrategy.authenticate` sets `opts.state` only when `__cliStateToken` exists (github.strategy.ts:59-62), and `githubAuthCallback` falls straight through to `setAuthCookies` when no `state` query param is present (auth.controller.ts:143-149). So a plain browser login has no CSRF/state parameter at any point: an attacker can complete the GitHub authorization dance and cause a victim's browser to be issued cookies for the attacker's account (forced login / session fixation) with nothing to detect it. docs/design/rest-api.md:381 as rewritten by this change reads as if that were covered ("minted per OAuth request … the guard above is the state token itself"), which is the "added-but-bypassable gate reads as covered" failure mode — the strongest entry point documented, the weakest one silent. The gap itself is pre-existing; the misleading claim is new here.

samples.summary: The login-binding nonce — now the only effective anti-injection secret — is printed to stderr and recorded in backend access logs
samples.evidence: login.ts:53-57 builds the start URL with `nonce=` and `code_challenge=` and prints it with `console.error`. This CLI's own README/design docs tell agents and CI to capture and parse stderr, so the nonce routinely lands in transcripts and job logs. On the server side the pino `req` serializer logs `url` (app.module.ts:68), and `customLogLevel` raises any 4xx/5xx on `/auth/github` to warn/error, so the nonce is written to production logs too. On its own this is ordinary OAuth practice (a nonce is not usually a bearer), but given the PKCE-downgrade gap above the nonce is the *sole* binding, so anyone with read access to those logs has the precondition for the code-injection chain. Mitigating this properly means fixing the PKCE enforcement rather than hiding the URL (which the headless copy-paste flow needs).

samples.summary: `backendErrorEnvelope` spreads arbitrary server-supplied fields into the machine-parsed stderr envelope, stripping only `command`
samples.evidence: Line 129 deletes only `command`; line 138 spreads every other key of the upstream `error` object (`{ ...fields, code, message, ... }`) into the single JSON line that, per the docs, agents parse and branch on. A hostile or compromised backend (or a MitM on a plain-HTTP self-hosted `--server`) can therefore inject arbitrary keys and arbitrary `message` text — including instruction-shaped text — into an agent's decision surface. The `command` anti-forgery carve-out shows the trust boundary was considered; an allow-list of forwarded fields (e.g. `code`, `message`, plus known context keys) would close the rest.

samples.summary: Server accepts and echoes a 1-character, arbitrary-charset `nonce`; no minimum entropy or alphabet restriction on the value it reflects into the loopback redirect
samples.evidence: `boundedToken(req.query?.nonce, 1, MAX_NONCE_LENGTH)` (github-auth.guard.ts:59) bounds only the length, unlike the challenge which also gets `/^[A-Za-z0-9\-._~]+$/`. The value is later reflected into the `Location` URL at auth.controller.ts:130-134; `encodeURIComponent` does prevent CRLF/parameter injection there, so the impact is limited to the server happily minting a state whose loopback binding is guessable for any client that picks a short nonce. Enforcing the same 43–128/base64url shape as the challenge would make the server's own guarantee independent of client discipline.

samples.summary: An unauthenticated loopback probe can flip the CLI's timeout message into attacker-chosen security advice ("the server may predate … or authenticate with `--api-key`")
samples.evidence: Any page in the victim's browser can issue `GET http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=x` with no `state`; that sets `sawUnboundCode = true` (login.ts:242) purely from attacker input. If the genuine callback then never arrives, the timeout text (login.ts:298-303) blames the server for predating the binding and steers the user toward `--api-key`. Attacker-controllable diagnostics that recommend an alternative auth path are a mild social-engineering lever; gate the message on a `state` that is absent *and* a code that came from the expected flow, or simply report both possibilities neutrally.

samples.summary: A wrong-verifier attempt burns the code, so anyone who learns a code can grief a legitimate login
samples.evidence: `consumeCode` deletes the entry before validating the verifier (cli-auth.store.ts:113, then 115-121). Burning on failure is the right call against guessing oracles, but it also means a party who observes a code in flight (loopback URL, browser history, proxy) can invalidate the victim's in-flight login with one bogus verifier, forcing a re-login. Low impact and arguably the correct trade-off; noting it so the trade-off is deliberate.

verdict.reason: The described code is present verbatim: consumeCode validates the PKCE verifier only when entry.codeChallenge is set (cli-auth.store.ts:115-121) and returns entry.userId when the entry has no challenge, even though a codeVerifier was supplied — the RFC 7636 §4.6 downgrade. The full attack chain is reachable in-repo: GitHubAuthGuard treats code_challenge as optional and still mints CLI state (github-auth.guard.ts:53-68), the callback copies the (undefined) challenge onto the code and redirects to the attacker-supplied loopback port echoing the attacker-supplied nonce (auth.controller.ts:126-135), the victim CLI accepts any code whose state matches its nonce (login.ts:240-246) and POSTs its verifier (login.ts:76-80), and cliExchange forwards to consumeCode which ignores that verifier and issues the attacker's tokens (auth.controller.ts:166-177). The nonce/port exposure premise also holds: the full OAuth URL including nonce is printed to stderr (login.ts:57) and req.url is logged verbatim by the pino serializer with only auth/cookie headers redacted (app.module.ts:65-83). No guard elsewhere requires a challenge for mode=cli, so PKCE is not the independent defence the docs assert (docs/design/rest-api.md:382, docs/design/cli.md:212-213). This is in the crypto/auth lane (verification skipped instead of enforced) and blocking as a clear security weakness.

verdict.reason: The described code exists exactly as claimed. `boundedToken` (github-auth.guard.ts:19-29) returns `undefined` for a `code_challenge` outside 43-128 chars or the base64url alphabet, and the guard then proceeds to `createState(mode, portNum, nonce, undefined)` (github-auth.guard.ts:56-67) and returns `super.canActivate(context)` — the authorization request is never failed. The `undefined` challenge propagates to the minted code (auth.controller.ts:126, cli-auth.store.ts:86-95), and `consumeCode` only enforces the verifier when a challenge was stored (cli-auth.store.ts:115-121), so the supplied `codeVerifier` is silently ignored and the code redeems as a plain bearer (auth.controller.ts:166). The CLI always sends a verifier and receives no signal that PKCE was dropped (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:45-56, 76-80), so the downgrade is unobservable at both ends; the nonce echo guards loopback binding only (login.ts:241-246), not code redeemability. I searched for an earlier rejection: no DTO/ValidationPipe covers these query params (main.ts:65-68 applies to decorated DTOs; githubAuth takes raw @Query strings, auth.controller.ts:84-95), and the guard's spec asserts the silent-drop behavior (github-auth.guard.spec.ts:88-109), so there is no upstream guard. This is a silently weakened auth/crypto binding — in-lane for the security lens and blocking at major severity.

verdict.reason: Verified in-repo: OAuth `state` is minted and validated only for the CLI path. github-auth.guard.ts:53 gates `createState` behind `mode === 'cli' && port`; github.strategy.ts:60-62 forwards `state` only when `__cliStateToken` exists, and the strategy's super() options (github.strategy.ts:43-49) set no `state`/`store`, so passport-oauth2 sends no state for browser logins. auth.controller.ts:119-149 validates state only inside the CLI branch and otherwise falls through directly to `setAuthCookies` + redirect. I searched wide for a counterexample and found none: auth.module.ts:29-30 registers no state store; `express-session` is a dependency (package.json:47) but no session/passport-session/stateStore middleware is initialized anywhere in packages/backend/src or main.ts; the web entry point (frontend login-form.tsx:27) sends no params, and the guard's own spec asserts no state is minted for it (github-auth.guard.spec.ts:114). Exploit chain is complete: attacker-obtained code replayed at /auth/github/callback via victim's browser yields victim-browser cookies for the attacker's account (login CSRF / session fixation, RFC 6749 §10.12); sameSite=lax (auth.controller.ts:271-278) does not block top-level GET navigation. docs/design/rest-api.md:381 as written ("minted per OAuth request … the guard above is the state token itself") describes this as covered, which is the added-but-bypassable-gate-reads-as-covered failure mode. In lane (crypto/auth: missing CSRF/state binding on the auth flow) and blocking at major severity.

searchedFor: glob packages/cli/test/*.ts — login-callback.test.ts no longer exists
finding.summary: CLI login callback accepts any `code` delivered to its loopback port — the state/nonce binding was removed, re-opening OAuth authorization-code injection (RFC 8252 §8.9)
finding.evidence:
`startCallbackServer()` (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:168-227) now takes no expected nonce and resolves the login promise with whatever `?code=` first arrives at `http://127.0.0.1:/callback` (line 177-182, resolve at line 225). There is no `state` check, no Origin/Host check, and the listener is reachable by any page in the user's browser (a cross-origin navigation/``/`fetch(no-cors)` to loopback still delivers the request; the response body is unreadable but the CLI has already consumed the code). Attack: attacker runs their own `GET /auth/github?mode=cli&port=` flow, captures a valid 60s single-use code minted for THEIR account, then has the victim's browser hit `http://127.0.0.1:

/callback?code=` for a spray of ephemeral ports while `wafflebase login` is waiting. The CLI exchanges it at `POST /auth/cli/exchange` (line 56) — which requires no other proof — and silently persists the attacker's session in `~/.wafflebase/session.json`; every subsequent `upload`/`docs create` writes the victim's data into the attacker's workspace. This delta deletes the exact mitigation (nonce mint, `state` echo, constant-time compare) plus its regression test `packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts`, so nothing in CI will notice.

verdict.reason: The finding claims the state/nonce binding was deleted from the CLI login callback, along with its regression test. Every named element is present in the working tree. packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:45 mints a 32-byte nonce and :46-49 mints a PKCE verifier/S256 challenge; :50 calls startCallbackServer(nonce), and the exported signature at :202 is startCallbackServer(expectedNonce: string) — directly contradicting "now takes no expected nonce". The handler at :240-246 reads ?state=, and on mismatch responds 400 'Invalid state' and returns without resolving; callbackResolve(code) at :289 is only reachable past that gate, so a code arriving with no/wrong state is never consumed. The comparison at :194-199 (nonceMatches) is a length check plus crypto.timingSafeEqual — the constant-time compare said to be removed. The exchange also carries codeVerifier (:79), so it is not "no other proof". The regression test the finding says was deleted exists: packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts:25-41 assert 400 for missing, wrong, and same-length-wrong state (defeating a length-only compare), :45-50 assert 200 and resolution only for the matching state, and :96-162 pin the start-URL wire format plus sha256(codeVerifier) == code_challenge. The backend cooperates: auth.controller.ts:127-134 echoes the CLI nonce back as &state=, and cli-auth.store.ts:115-121 rejects an exchange whose verifier does not hash to the stored challenge via secretEquals. The narrated attack (spraying an attacker-minted code at guessed loopback ports) is refused at login.ts:241 and would additionally fail PKCE at cli-auth.store.ts:120.

mergedFrom.summary: `POST /auth/cli/exchange` has no proof-of-possession: the nonce now available server-side is not required to redeem the code

finding.summary: CLI auth code is still not bound to the client (no PKCE); the nonce only gates the local listener, so an intercepted code is fully redeemable
finding.evidence: The change cites RFC 8252 §8.9, whose actual prescription for the loopback-redirect code-injection problem is PKCE. What landed is a `state` echo checked only inside the CLI's own listener (`packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:206`). The code itself remains an unbound bearer: `POST /auth/cli/exchange` (auth.controller.ts:152-168) takes `{ code }` with no authentication, no `code_verifier`, and no reference to the nonce — `consumeCode` looks up only the code (cli-auth.store.ts:71). Attack: anyone who observes the code within its 60s TTL — from the victim's browser history/URL bar (`http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=…` is a real navigation), a browser extension, a shared/kiosk machine, or an intercepting proxy — POSTs it to /auth/cli/exchange and receives the victim's `accessToken` + `refreshToken`. The nonce does nothing here because the CLI listener is not in the path. Grepped the whole repo for pkce/code_verifier/code_challenge: zero hits. Severity is 'major' rather than 'critical' because it needs code interception, and confidence is low because I could not demonstrate a concrete interception channel in this codebase.

verdict.reason: The finding claims the CLI auth code is not bound to the client (no PKCE), and that grepping the repo for pkce/code_verifier/code_challenge gives zero hits. Both are false here: full RFC 7636 S256 PKCE is implemented end-to-end. (1) The CLI mints a verifier that never leaves the process and sends only its S256 hash: login.ts:46-49 derives codeChallenge, line 56 appends &code_challenge=. (2) The backend binds it to the login state: github-auth.guard.ts:61 reads req.query.code_challenge, bounds it to 43-128 chars with a restricted charset, and passes it to createState (cli-auth.store.ts:42-60 stores codeChallenge). (3) The challenge rides onto the authorization code: auth.controller.ts:126 calls createCode(user.id, state.codeChallenge), stored on CodeEntry at cli-auth.store.ts:86-95. (4) Exchange requires the verifier: auth.controller.ts:166 passes body.codeVerifier (DTO-validated at auth.dto.ts:13-16) into consumeCode, and cli-auth.store.ts:115-121 returns undefined when a stored challenge exists and the verifier is missing or its sha256/base64url digest mismatches, compared in constant time via secretEquals (cli-auth.store.ts:31-35) after the code is already deleted (line 113), so it is not an existence oracle. (5) The CLI supplies it at login.ts:79 as { code, codeVerifier }. The described attack therefore fails: a code observed in browser history, by an extension, on a kiosk, or via a proxy is not redeemable without the verifier, which never went on the wire. Downgrading to the legacy no-challenge branch is not attacker-reachable, since the challenge is bound at authorization time from the victim's own request rather than asserted at exchange time; that branch only applies to codes minted by a CLI that sent no challenge, which the current CLI never does. The nonce echo (auth.controller.ts:130-134, login.ts:241) is a second independent binding, not the only protection, contradicting the finding's core premise. Tests cover this at auth.controller.spec.ts:364-392 and packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts:141-160.
